draft.briefing: Hey, you're at Cubbon Park! It started in 1870 as a 100 acre park and has grown to around 300 acres right in the middle of the city. It's been renamed twice, and its official name today is Sri Chamarajendra Park.
draft.hungryLine: You're close to some Bengaluru classics, from biryani on a banana leaf to the famous Death by Chocolate sundae on Residency Rd.

moodReplies.show-me-around: The Venkatappa Art Gallery and the red Karnataka High Court are both a 7 min walk, and the Visvesvaraya Industrial and Technological Museum is about 8 minutes away.
moodReplies.somewhere-to-chill: Find a shady spot under the old trees in Cubbon Park itself, just a couple of minutes from here.
moodReplies.surprise-me: The park was first called Meade's Park, after acting commissioner Sir John Meade. It became Cubbon Park when he left for Baroda in 1873.

tips.title: Walk the park early.
tips.body: Mornings are the coolest and calmest time to enjoy the trees and lawns.

tips.title: Expect two ticket prices.
tips.body: Bengaluru attractions often charge foreigners a lot more than locals.

story.title: Siege of Bangalore
story.body: In the Third Anglo-Mysore War, Cornwallis took the town on 7 February while Tipu Sultan harried his camps. After six weeks of siege the British stormed the fort on 21 March.

story.title: A park is born
story.body: Major General Richard Sankey, the British Chief Engineer of Mysore State, laid out a 100 acre park here. It was first named Meade's Park after the acting commissioner.

story.title: Cubbon Park
story.body: When Meade left for Baroda, the park was renamed after Sir Mark Cubbon, the longest-serving commissioner of the time.

story.title: Sri Chamarajendra Park
story.body: To mark the Silver Jubilee of Sri Krishnaraja Wodeyar's rule, it was renamed again after Sri Chamarajendra Wodeyar, under whose rule the park first came about.

story.title: A museum in the park
story.body: Jawaharlal Nehru opened the Visvesvaraya Industrial and Technological Museum inside the park on July 14, 1962, in memory of Sir M. Visvesvaraya.
